blocks.heading: Activities in Namibia
blocks.text: Namibia's leisure and tourist activities use its landscapes, wildlife and culture. Visitors climb the red dunes and take photographs at Sossusvlei in the Namib-Naukluft National Park. Hikers walk the Fish River Canyon trail in the south during the cooler months, roughly May to mid-September. The coastal resort of Swakopmund offers quad biking, skydiving and beach holidays. Wildlife viewing takes place in national parks and in communal conservancies.

Etosha National Park in northern Namibia was first proclaimed in 1907 and covers about 22,000 km². It is dominated by the Etosha Pan, a large salt pan that is usually dry, so wildlife depends on waterholes. Visitors take game drives, bird-watch and photograph animals at waterholes, including floodlit ones at the Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni rest camps, which provide chalets, camping, restaurants and guided drives.

Heritage visits include Twyfelfontein in the Kunene Region, Namibia's first World Heritage Site (2007), where guides show visitors ancient rock engravings. Community-based tourism offers guiding, craft sales, campsites and joint-venture lodges in conservancies, giving local people income from wildlife and culture when they control what is shared.

Residents also use local leisure facilities such as sports fields, parks and braai sites, and make holiday trips to the coast. Each activity needs particular services: hiking trails need path maintenance, game drives need roads and rules, and overnight stays need water and waste services. When describing an activity, name the place, the activity and the resource it uses, for example game drives in Etosha using its wildlife, or dune climbing at Sossusvlei using desert scenery.
